Press enter or click to view image in full size UX Artificial Intelligence Product Design Cloud Computing Product Strategy Buying shoes you can’t try on Selen Şentürk 19 min read · Oct 9, 2026 -- 2 Listen Share You want to train a mid-sized model on your own data. The model is chosen, the data is ready, the code runs. The only thing missing is a machine to run it on. So you open a GPU platform’s pricing page. What you get is a shelf. Seventy-nine models grouped under eleven headings, and the headings read: Blackwell, Ada Lovelace, Ampere, Turing, Volta, Pascal, Maxwell. Those are a chip vendor’s generation codenames. On another platform the same shelf is sorted by memory capacity. On a third, a single page lists a hundred and sixty-two server series, twenty-three of which are GPU series. You scroll. Not one heading asks your question. Your question is: my model is this, my data is this size, what should I rent and what will it cost me. Worth noticing something here. The person opening this page is technical. They write code, they train models, they live in a terminal. The problem is not a lack of knowledge. The shelf is full, the person is capable, and nobody has done the translation in between. This gap is not new. Twenty years ago the same gap existed in a far more ordinary product, and it got solved. How shoes got sold without a fitting room People did not use to buy shoes without putting them on. Today they do, without hesitating. Technology is not what made that possible. Showing shoes over the internet was never the hard part. The hard part was working out what trying them on actually did in the buyer’s head. It did three things: it confirmed the size fit, it revealed how the shoe was cut, and it removed the risk of choosing wrong. You knew before you left the store. What e-commerce did was take those three functions apart and move each one somewhere else. Size confirmation went to the size chart. Fit information went to other buyers’ reviews, because only someone who has worn the shoe can tell you it runs narrow. And the risk went to free returns. That last one matters most and gets discussed least. What made buying-without-trying possible was not the size chart. It was the seller absorbing the cost of a wrong choice. The trying-on step did not disappear. It moved from before the purchase to after it. There is one more thing, and it is the important one. None of this was solved by copying the warehouse onto the screen. In a warehouse, shoes sit by box number, by season, by supplier. That order is correct for shipping. But no shop ever arranged its window by box number, because that is not the order in the customer’s head. That was the whole of it. Don’t show the customer how the warehouse is organised. Rebuild, on the screen, the order that is already in their head. And in GPU clouds, the opposite is happening. Whose order is on the screen We are going to look at five screens. Whichever platform you pick, a hyperscaler, an independent GPU cloud, or a marketplace, the same thing happens on all five. Their being shared is the point. If it showed up in one group it would be those companies’ choice. Showing up across all of them makes it the field’s own habit. And on all five it is the same thing: the screen shows the company’s internal order. How the stock records are kept, how the billing system is split, how capacity gets handed out, what the steps of the sales process are. Not the order in the customer’s head. The catalog, in the warehouse’s order Look at what they are sorted by. You will find five different schemes: memory capacity, chip architecture codename, vendor product name, the provider’s own internal series code, and letter-based server families. All five are correct orders. But they are correct for the side keeping stock, not the side buying. A data centre keeps its inventory this way, because there the thing being counted is a machine. The catalog is those stock records, put on a screen. What the customer is counting is not a machine. It is a job. “I am training this model on this data.” Something has to translate between the two, and nobody has done it. Two partial exceptions exist off to the side, a line of guidance on some rows and a task tab in a calculator, but both sit outside the main catalog. The filter panel has the same problem. At one provider, seeing a single price means first choosing an operating system, a category, a server series, a region, a currency, and a pricing model. Six decisions, and none of the six helps you find what you came for. All six exist to shorten the list. That is not a search. It is a records lookup the customer has been made to run. This is where e-commerce’s most basic distinction gets missed. A person who knows what they want uses search. A person who does not browses categories. Two screens, two mental states. GPU platforms have built only for the first group, and even that is not really a search, just a flat list. Behind it sits a familiar design principle: people are better at recognition than at recall.
